title: Why a Game AI Should Leave You an Opening | Game Design

scenes.title: 상대를 이기는 것보다 중요한 것
lines: Mario's punch can connect at close range, while a distant incoming attack can leave room to dodge. Would a computer that responds perfectly to every situation be a good opponent?
We will examine the information and decisions that move an opponent, look at why dice can feel unfair, and work toward computer opponents that are challenging but beatable.

scenes.title: 움직임과 사람다운 판단
lines: Old attract-mode demonstrations could make a character move, yet still attack in the wrong place or walk into danger. Producing movement and reading a situation like a person are different problems.
A computer-controlled player is often labeled CP or CPU. More freedom of action means more situations to handle. But if its reactions are excessively fast, players can feel the match is unfair.

scenes.title: 주사위까지 상대편인 느낌
lines: That suspicion is not limited to action games. In a dice-driven game such as Dicey Dungeons, a favorable enemy roll can feel as though the computer chose an advantage.

The same computer handles the roll and selects the opponent's action. That makes even results within the rules easy to distrust. Designers need to consider both fairness in the rules and fairness as players experience it.

scenes.title: 상황을 데이터로 읽기
lines: As the available choices multiply, building an opponent that chooses well becomes harder. Free movement and varied attacks make Super Smash Bros. Ultimate a clear example. Those opponents are essential when players want to enjoy battles alone.

Here, attacks try to launch the opponent off the stage. The percentage below a fighter is accumulated damage, rather than remaining health; higher damage generally makes the fighter easier to launch farther.
The computer does not have a person's eyes. The game supplies data such as position, health, and state, and uses that information to select its next action.
It needs to know an attack's reach and timing, and how far a move carries the character. Comparing those with the opponent's attacks helps it choose a response.

scenes.title: 거리 하나가 행동을 바꾸기
lines: In our model, suppose an attack reaches two spaces but the opponent is three spaces away. Swinging from that position will miss. Moving one space closer or selecting a longer-range attack is a better choice.
The same attack can be a different choice when the opponent approaches or is already committed to another move. Believable movement requires those conditions to work together.

scenes.title: 변하는 상태와 겹치는 판단
lines: Behavior can also change with the flow of a match. A character might become more aggressive at low health, maintain a preferred distance, or adapt its movement to its speed and jump height.
Some games also adjust their intensity when one side pulls too far ahead. As conditions accumulate, different decisions become more likely to collide at the same moment.

What if one condition says to approach and attack while another says to retreat from danger? Without a priority, the character can stop or hesitate back and forth. Its design needs both a decision priority and conditions for switching actions.

scenes.title: 반응할 시간과 실수
lines: An accurate decision does not have to execute immediately. Super Smash Bros. Ultimate gives its CPUs a reaction delay so they do not instantly respond to every sudden event like a machine.
At sixty frames per second in our model, waiting twelve frames means waiting two tenths of a second. A gap like this can separate noticing an event from acting on it.
Its CPUs can also show a little confusion when an effect reverses their controls. Their behavior makes the changed state visible, without leaving them permanently helpless or repeatedly falling away.

scenes.title: 공격하는 상대가 남기는 빈틈
lines: The game also tuned its CPUs to be more aggressive than in earlier entries. Rather than having them defend and evade perfectly, it encourages attacks, giving the player chances to read and answer those actions.
Committing to an attack also creates an opening. The player can make it miss by controlling distance, then move in and counter after the attack ends.

scenes.title: 이길 수 없는 상대보다
lines: Return to our opening question. An opponent that blocks and dodges correctly every time does not automatically make the match enjoyable.

It needs useful information, decisions that do not contradict one another, time for the player to respond, and openings to exploit. A computer opponent's goal is to create a good contest, rather than win at any cost.
